publications.assertionSummary: Banks's Bury attribution is consistent with Candidate B and most plausibly tracked the Newgate apprentice

incoming.explanation: The p.151 'Banks Mss.' entry is the datum the finding interprets.
Newgate's Horningsheath/Bury origin supplies the mechanism by which a Bury tag attaches to the apprentice, not the emigrant.
No Bury natal household survives, so the attribution cannot be a birth record.

Parallels Banks's Bury St Edmunds attribution, another named compiler tradition that likewise proved to be a mistaken pointer at the Newgate apprentice rather than a proof or disproof of the Norfolk origin.

The Chaplin will illustrates the genuine Bury St Edmunds/New England traffic behind Banks's attribution - a Bury Gurney servant in a household tied to Boston through the Houchin debt - without connecting to any John Gurney or natal household, consistent with the unit's reading of 'Bury' as a real migration corridor mis-applied to the emigrant.

outgoing.explanation: The finding rests on the identity work's de-conflation of the 1636 Newgate apprentice from the Braintree emigrant (trade-and-training G13-RI-000075).

finding.shortLabel: Banks's Bury attribution is an unproven lead that most plausibly tracked Newgate's apprentice; consistent with a Norfolk origin

sources.locator: p. 158, John Gurney entry: English origin given as 'Unknown'

finding.statement: Banks's 'Bury St Edmunds' is an unproven lead, not a birthplace - and it is consistent with the favoured Norfolk (Candidate B) origin rather than evidence against it. Sourced only to 'Banks Mss.', with no supporting Bury natal record found, the attribution is best explained by the 1636 apprentice John Gurney whom the Bury-area feltmaker John Newgate brought before the Boston court: that younger man, de-conflated from the Braintree emigrant in the identity work, carried the Bury/Suffolk association, and Banks's memo most plausibly tracked him. Anderson's Great Migration Directory (p. 158) independently declines Banks, entering the origin as 'Unknown'. A Norwich-born son of Francis Gurney who trained at or near Bury would fit Banks's note without contradiction.

finding.shortLabel: Thomas Chaplin's 1672 Bury will: 40 pounds to 'Mary Gurney my servant' beside a New England (Houchin) debt

sources.alignmentNote: Muskett's abstract of the 1672 Chaplin will: '40 pounds to Mary Gurney my servant'; the Jeremy Houchin New England debt.
sources.locator: vol. 3 pt. 1, 'Chaplin of Semer, Bury, etc.' pedigree, printed p. ~109 (will of Thomas Chaplin of Bury St Edmunds, 24 Apr. 1672, proved 25 Nov. 1672, Arch. Sudbury reg. 1672 fo. 349)

finding.statement: Thomas Chaplin of Bury St Edmunds, gent., 'being aged,' in his will dated 24 April 1672 (proved 25 November 1672, Archdeaconry of Sudbury) left 40 pounds 'to Mary Gurney my servant' - an extraordinary legacy for a servant, eight times the 5 pounds he left his own daughter Abigail Whiteing - and in the same will directed that a debt owing from 'Jeremy Houchin, late in New England' be collected and 60 pounds of it divided among his Shepherd grandchildren. The will places a Bury St Edmunds Gurney woman in service in 1672, in a household directly tied to Boston through the Houchin debt - a concrete instance of the Bury/New England traffic Banks's attribution gestured at. It names no John Gurney and connects to no identified natal household; its bearing is on the Suffolk-migration milieu, not on the emigrant's parentage.
